defaults.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.
defaults.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life

questions.scenario: A glass is filled to the very brim with water, with ice cubes floating in it.
questions.question: When all the ice melts, what happens?
questions.reveal: The level stays the same; nothing overflows.
questions.explanation: Floating ice displaces exactly its own weight of water. When it melts, it becomes exactly that weight of liquid water, which fills precisely the space the ice was pushing aside below the waterline. The bit of ice poking above the surface is just making up for ice being less dense than water. So the level doesn't change.
questions.intuitionTrap: The ice sticking up above the surface looks like extra volume waiting to spill over.
questions.principle: A floating object displaces its own weight of liquid (Archimedes' principle).
questions.caveat: This holds for pure water with freely floating ice; small temperature-related volume changes can nudge it very slightly.
questions.funFact: That's why melting floating sea ice barely raises sea level, while melting land ice does.

questions.scenario: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been lying side by side on a table in the same room all day. You pick up one in each hand.
questions.question: Which spoon is actually colder?
questions.explanation: After hours in the same room, both spoons are at room temperature. The metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your warm fingers much faster. Your skin doesn't sense temperature directly; it senses how quickly heat is flowing in or out. Wood conducts heat poorly, so the patch you touch quickly warms toward skin temperature and feels neutral.
questions.intuitionTrap: We trust our sense of touch as a thermometer.
questions.principle: Touch senses heat flow, which depends on a material's thermal conductivity, not just its temperature.
questions.funFact: The same effect is why a tiled bathroom floor feels freezing while a rug in the same room feels fine.

questions.scenario: You pour an ice-cold drink into a glass. A few minutes later, the outside of the glass is wet.
questions.question: Where did that water come from?
questions.reveal: From water vapour in the surrounding air.
questions.explanation: Air always contains invisible water vapour. When air touches the cold surface of the glass, it cools below its 'dew point', the temperature at which it can't hold all its vapour, and the excess condenses into droplets. Glass is waterproof, so nothing leaks through. On a humid day the glass gets wetter; in a dry room it may stay almost dry.
questions.intuitionTrap: Water on the outside of a container full of liquid looks like a leak.
questions.principle: Air cooled below its dew point releases water vapour as liquid condensation.
questions.funFact: It's the same physics that makes morning dew, fog and the drips from an air conditioner.

questions.scenario: On a hot day, you shut yourself in a small, closed room with a refrigerator and leave the fridge door wide open.
questions.question: Over an hour, what happens to the room's temperature?
questions.explanation: A refrigerator doesn't destroy heat; it pumps heat from inside the box out through the coils at the back. With the door open, it's moving heat from the room... into the same room. Meanwhile its motor turns electrical energy into extra heat. Net result: the room gets slightly warmer. Air conditioners only cool a room because they dump their heat outdoors.
questions.intuitionTrap: The cold air pouring out of the door feels like cooling.
questions.principle: Refrigerators are heat pumps; they move heat and add the energy they consume as extra heat.
questions.funFact: The coils on the back of a fridge release more heat than the fridge removes from its contents, because they also dump the motor's energy.

questions.scenario: On a hot, sunny, breezy day in the desert, you wear a loose black robe instead of a loose white one.
questions.question: Will you necessarily end up hotter?
options: No, black always keeps you cooler
questions.explanation: A black robe does absorb more sunlight, and its outer surface gets noticeably hotter. But a 1980 study of Bedouin robes found that the heat reaching the wearer's body was about the same with black and white. The hotter fabric warms the air beneath it, which rises and pulls in fresh air through the loose weave and openings, carrying extra heat away, especially when there's a breeze.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Black absorbs heat' is true, so it seems to settle the question.
questions.principle: What reaches your skin depends on absorption, airflow and convection together, not colour alone.
questions.caveat: Tight black clothing in still air is a different story: then it can make you noticeably warmer.
questions.funFact: The researchers even tested robes on volunteers standing in the Negev desert at midday.

questions.scenario: You microwave a cup of cold liquid water and a block of ice of the same mass, side by side, for the same short time.
questions.question: Which absorbs microwave energy faster?
questions.explanation: Microwaves heat food mainly by making water molecules twist back and forth as the field flips billions of times a second. In liquid water, molecules can rotate fairly freely and absorb that energy well. In ice, they're locked into a crystal and can barely rotate, so ice absorbs microwaves poorly. That's why defrost settings pulse on and off: they let small thawed areas spread heat into frozen parts instead of cooking the edges.
questions.intuitionTrap: If microwaves 'heat water', frozen water seems like it should heat just as well.
questions.principle: Microwave heating depends on how easily molecules can rotate in the oscillating field (dielectric loss).
questions.funFact: Most microwave ovens operate at about 2.45 GHz, the same band as many Wi-Fi networks.

questions.scenario: Dal that takes an hour in an open pot is ready in minutes in a pressure cooker.
questions.question: Why does the pressure cooker cook so much faster?
questions.reveal: The water inside gets hotter than 100 °C.
questions.explanation: In an open pot, water can't get hotter than its boiling point, about 100 °C at sea level; extra heat just makes more steam. Sealing the lid traps the steam and raises the pressure to roughly double normal air pressure, which pushes the boiling point up to around 120 °C. Cooking reactions speed up a lot with every extra degree, so food softens in a fraction of the time.
questions.intuitionTrap: Pressure itself seems to be doing the cooking.
questions.principle: Higher pressure raises water's boiling point, allowing hotter cooking temperatures.
questions.funFact: Pressure cookers matter even more at altitude, where water in an open pot boils well below 100 °C.

questions.scenario: A moving bicycle stays upright far more easily than one that is standing still.
questions.question: What is mainly responsible?
options: It steers itself under its lean
questions.reveal: It steers itself back under its lean.
questions.explanation: Gyroscopic effects exist but are small. A moving bike stays up mainly because, when it starts to lean, its front wheel turns toward the lean, steering the wheels back under the centre of mass, much as you balance a broom on your palm by moving your hand. In 2011, researchers built a bicycle with extra counter-spinning wheels to cancel the gyroscopic effect, and it still balanced itself.
questions.intuitionTrap: Spinning wheels look like gyroscopes, so gyroscopes get the credit.
questions.principle: Bicycle stability comes mostly from steering geometry and mass distribution that steer the bike into its fall.
questions.funFact: Riders do the same thing unconsciously: to turn left, you briefly steer right so the bike leans left.

questions.scenario: You fill your car tyres to the right pressure on a warm afternoon. The next morning is much colder.
questions.question: What does the tyre gauge read in the cold morning?
questions.explanation: The air in a tyre is a fixed amount of gas in a nearly fixed volume. Its pressure comes from molecules hitting the tyre walls, and colder molecules move more slowly and hit less hard. So when the temperature drops, the pressure drops with it, by roughly 1 psi for every 5–6 °C. Nothing leaked; check tyre pressures when the tyres are cold for an accurate reading.
questions.intuitionTrap: If no air escaped, the pressure seems like it should stay put.
questions.principle: For a fixed amount of gas in a fixed volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.
questions.funFact: Formula 1 teams warm their tyres in electric blankets before a race partly to get pressures right.

questions.scenario: Soap bubbles shimmer with swirling rainbow colours, even though soapy water is colourless.
questions.question: Where do the colours come from?
questions.reveal: Light reflecting off both surfaces of the film and interfering.
questions.explanation: A bubble's wall is a film only a few hundred nanometres thick. Light reflects from both its outer and inner surfaces, and the two reflections overlap. Depending on the film's thickness, some colours line up and reinforce each other while others cancel out. As the film drains and thins, the colours swirl and shift, and just before popping it can turn almost black.
questions.intuitionTrap: Rainbows are linked with prisms and raindrops, so we assume the same splitting of light.
questions.principle: Thin-film interference: light reflected from two nearby surfaces reinforces or cancels by wavelength.
questions.funFact: The same effect colours oil slicks on wet roads and some beetle shells and butterfly wings.

questions.scenario: A tennis player hits a ball with heavy topspin, so the top of the ball rotates forward as it flies.
questions.question: Compared with a ball hit the same way with no spin, what does it do?
questions.explanation: A spinning ball drags a thin layer of air around with it. With topspin, the airflow leaving the back of the ball gets deflected upward, and by Newton's third law the ball is pushed downward. This Magnus effect makes topspin shots dive into the court, letting players hit hard and still land the ball in. Backspin does the opposite and makes the ball float.
questions.intuitionTrap: Spin feels like a cosmetic extra that shouldn't change where a ball goes.
questions.principle: The Magnus effect: a spinning ball deflects air to one side and feels a force toward the other.
questions.funFact: Golf balls fly far partly thanks to backspin, which creates lift; their dimples help keep that airflow attached.

questions.scenario: You add a spoonful of salt to a big pot of water on the stove before cooking pasta.
questions.question: What does the salt do to the water's boiling point?
questions.reveal: It raises it, but only by a tiny fraction of a degree.
questions.explanation: Dissolved particles make water molecules slightly less likely to escape as vapour, so salt raises the boiling point. But a cooking amount of salt in a big pot raises it by only a small fraction of a degree, so it doesn't speed up or slow down boiling in any useful way. The burst of bubbles when salt hits hot water is just dissolved gas escaping onto the crystals. Salt is for flavour.
questions.intuitionTrap: The fizz when salt goes in looks like it's making the water boil.
questions.principle: Solutes raise a solvent's boiling point in proportion to their concentration (boiling-point elevation).
questions.funFact: To raise water's boiling point by even 1 °C, you'd need roughly 50 grams of salt per litre, saltier than seawater.

questions.scenario: Aluminium foil has a shiny side and a dull side.
questions.question: For ordinary cooking, does it matter which side faces the food?
questions.explanation: The two sides differ only because of how foil is made. In the final rolling step, two sheets pass through the rollers together: the sides touching the polished rollers come out shiny, and the sides touching each other come out matte. The difference in how much heat they reflect is small, so for normal cooking it makes no meaningful difference which way you wrap.
questions.intuitionTrap: Two visibly different sides seem like they must have two different jobs.
questions.principle: Surface finish from manufacturing slightly changes reflectivity, but the effect on cooking is negligible.
questions.caveat: Non-stick foil is different: it has a coating on one side, which should face the food.
questions.funFact: Household foil is typically less than a fiftieth of a millimetre thick.

questions.scenario: Some old church windows are thicker at the bottom than at the top.
questions.question: Is that because glass slowly flows downward over centuries?
options: Yes, glass is a very slow liquid
No, it was made that way
Yes, but only in hot climates
questions.reveal: No; it was made uneven to begin with.
questions.explanation: At room temperature glass is an amorphous solid: its atoms are disordered like a liquid's, but locked in place. Calculations suggest any flow at room temperature would take vastly longer than the age of the universe to notice. Old windowpanes were made by methods such as spinning molten glass into a disc, which produced uneven sheets. Installers often put the thick edge at the bottom, but sometimes at the top or side.
questions.intuitionTrap: Uneven old glass looks like evidence of slow dripping.
questions.principle: Glass is an amorphous solid with an astronomically high viscosity at room temperature.
questions.funFact: Ancient Roman glassware and centuries-old telescope lenses show no sign of sagging.

questions.scenario: A driver who brakes hard from 50 km/h stops in a certain distance after the brakes bite.
questions.question: From 100 km/h, on the same road with the same brakes, how far does the braking take?
questions.explanation: Brakes remove kinetic energy, and kinetic energy grows with the square of speed. Double the speed and there's four times as much energy to get rid of, so with the same braking force the car needs about four times the distance. On top of that, the distance covered during the driver's reaction time simply doubles. Speed matters far more than it feels like it should.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect stopping distance to grow in step with speed: twice as fast, twice as far.
questions.principle: Kinetic energy = ½mv², so braking distance grows with the square of speed.
questions.funFact: Hitting something at 60 km/h carries about the same energy as falling from a 14-metre building, roughly four storeys.

goDeeper.text: With constant deceleration a, going from 50 to 100 km/h multiplies v² and therefore d by 4.

questions.scenario: A thermometer reads 34 °C on two days. One day is dry; the other is very humid.
questions.question: Why does the humid day feel so much worse?
options: Humid air presses on your skin
questions.reveal: Your sweat can't evaporate as easily.
questions.explanation: Your body's main way of cooling in heat is sweating: as sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your skin. When the air is already loaded with water vapour, evaporation slows down, so sweat drips instead of cooling you. Your body keeps heating up at the same air temperature. That's why weather services report a 'feels like' or heat index temperature.
questions.intuitionTrap: If the thermometer reads the same, the heat seems like it should feel the same.
questions.principle: Evaporation absorbs latent heat; it slows when the surrounding air is close to saturated.
questions.funFact: Dogs pant for the same reason: evaporating water from their tongue and airways cools them down.

questions.scenario: Chain round. You drop a single ice cube into a glass of room-temperature water.
questions.question: What does the cube do first?
questions.reveal: It floats, with about nine-tenths underwater.
questions.explanation: Water is unusual: its solid is less dense than its liquid. As water freezes, its molecules lock into an open hexagonal lattice held apart by hydrogen bonds, so ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water. That's enough to float, but only just, so roughly nine-tenths of the cube sits below the waterline, exactly as with an iceberg.
questions.intuitionTrap: Solids are usually denser than their liquids, so a frozen lump seems like it should sink.
questions.principle: Ice is less dense than liquid water, and a floating object sinks until it displaces its own weight.
questions.funFact: If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and much of the life in them could not survive winter.

questions.scenario: Chain round, continued. As the floating cube melts, it releases a trickle of very cold meltwater, close to 0 °C.
questions.question: Where does that cold meltwater go?
questions.explanation: Cold liquid water near 0 °C is denser than room-temperature water, so the meltwater sinks, pulling warmer water in to replace it. That sets up a slow circulation that carries heat to the cube and speeds its melting. You can see it by using a coloured ice cube: streamers of colour drift downward. Ice floats, but its meltwater dives.
questions.intuitionTrap: Since the ice floats, it seems like its meltwater should float too.
questions.principle: Between about 4 °C and room temperature, colder water is denser than warmer water.
questions.caveat: Water is densest at about 4 °C; in water colder than that, meltwater would rise instead.
questions.funFact: This density quirk keeps the bottom of deep lakes at about 4 °C all winter.

questions.scenario: Chain round, finale. You marked the water level on the glass just after the ice cube went in. Now the cube has completely melted.
questions.question: Compared with your mark, where is the water level now?
questions.explanation: While floating, the cube displaced exactly its own weight of water. Melting turns it into exactly that weight of water, which fills the space it was displacing. The part above the waterline only existed because ice is less dense; once it's liquid, that extra volume disappears. So the level ends where it started after the cube went in.
questions.intuitionTrap: The visible ice above the waterline looks like extra water still to come.
questions.principle: A floating object displaces its own weight of liquid (Archimedes' principle).
questions.funFact: You've now followed the cube from floating, through sinking meltwater, to a level that never moved.
